prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Context: National Airspace System (NAS); air traffic management (ATM); Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), controllers, pilots, airspace users, stakeholders, aircraft, automation.
Current ATM predicts trajectories from approved flight plans and scheduled/controlled departure times. Conservative strategic management changes flight plans; controllers tactically issue “open trajectory” vectors, altitude changes, and speed clearances for separation, weather avoidance, and NAS/Traffic Flow Management (TFM) restrictions. Actions are not directly communicated to stakeholders/automation; prediction-data/model gaps and disruptions obscure downstream delays and resource demand.
Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times targeting a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) at a NAS constraint, using airspace-user estimated en-route time without other controller-action knowledge. Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) assumes accurate estimated times of arrival (ETAs).
Future: Management by Trajectory (MBT) has FAA and airspace users negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all flights, communicating traffic-management plans. Assigned trajectories must respect user goals and all known NAS constraints from current location to destination; constraint impacts become trajectory constraints. MBT accommodates commercial aviation, Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, and on-demand air transportation vehicles, including expanding anticipated operations.
Pilots and air traffic controllers use automation to maintain assigned trajectories, including temporal/speed constraints. Equipped aircraft bear substantial compliance responsibility without controller intervention. Ground-based/aircraft automation improvements and air-ground/ground-stakeholder data communications enable MBT.
MBT eliminates most unpredictable local reactive actions. Uncertainty/disruption resolutions should modify trajectories as early as possible; remaining trajectory-constraint adjustments are proactive to maximize predictability.
Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) means either a NAS vision with 4DT-centered air traffic control/management or evolving endeavors advancing that vision. MBT resembles TBO concepts employing a four-dimensional (4D) contract. Appendix “Comparison with ICAO TBO Concept” compares MBT with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO concept.

U0027: MBT is one specific interpretation of the high-level TBO vision, and is the starting point from which specific challenges can be identified and studied, contributing to the refinement of the MBT concept and the overall body of knowledge related to TBO. 1.1 NAS Shortfalls Addressed by MBT This section summarizes the shortfalls in the current NAS that are addressed by MBT, as shown in Table 1.
U0028: These shortfalls are consistent with those identified in the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO Concept Document [1].
U0029: The ICAO TBO Concept Document provides high-level guidance for resolving these shortfalls, and the MBT concept provides a specific vision for resolving the shortfalls that is consistent with the ICAO TBO Concept.
U0030: Table 1.
U0031: NAS Shortfalls Addressed by MBT Shortfalls MBT Improvements Data exchanged between airspace users and the FAA are too sparse to support accurate trajectory prediction across all phases of flight and trajectory synchronization across automation systems.
U0032: The data needed by all relevant airspace users, aircraft, and FAA automation systems to develop accurate, consistent 4DT predictions are available to all relevant systems.
U0033: The use of open trajectories, including tactical maneuvers, causes poor trajectory predictability.
U0034: Aircraft operate on closed trajectories to the extent possible, which improves trajectory predictability.
U0035: Insufficient publication of trajectory changes and lack of trajectory synchronization result in poor trajectory predictability.
U0036: Publication of all trajectory changes and advanced exchange of trajectory information between ground automation systems and the aircraft allow for trajectory synchronization across systems, resulting in consistent trajectory predictions across systems.
U0037: Poor trajectory predictability inhibits strategic (longer look ahead) trajectory management.
U0038: Improved trajectory predictability, improved coordination capabilities, and use of 4DTs enable controllers to use strategic, closed clearances.
U0039: A high level of trajectory predictability becomes the new norm.
U0040: Enhanced predictability will improve TFM performance and provide a more consistent flow of air traffic, where demand will more accurately meet available capacity, reducing or eliminating delay.
